findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an automated enforcement mechanism (e.g. a required CI status check that reads recorded gate metadata, or a branch-protection rule keyed on a gate-passing label) so that A2-2 and A6-1 cannot be merged/executed if the 24-hour descendant-workflow evidence is absent, reducing reliance on contributor process discipline alone.
evidence: Plan quote: 'Record the A2-1 merge SHA, workflow run id, and git merge-base --is-ancestor result on A2-2 before merge. This is the concrete writer-rollout signal; no pass-record version stamp exists.'
The gate is described entirely as a recording/documentation step on the PR, with no mention of a required CI status check or automated branch-protection rule that would block an out-of-order merge.

The identical pattern is used for A6-1 ('A6-1 may not begin until A6-0a has been merged to main for at least 24 hours'), where a premature start would execute the irreversible history rewrite before the epoch guard is deployed.
findings.finding: The 24-hour descendant-workflow gate for A2-2 (and the identical gate for A6-1) is enforced only by process discipline: the plan requires the author to manually record the merge SHA, workflow run ID, and merge-base output on the PR before merge, but no CI check, branch-protection rule, or automated gate blocks an early merge. If a contributor merges A2-2 before A2-1's new-location writer has been executed by a real workflow run, old-format readers that consumed the legacy inline `last_get_pass` field would silently fall back to zero, resetting rotation state mid-operation — exactly the race the gate is designed to prevent.
findings.location: Observable rollout gates section — 'A2-2 may not merge until A2-1 has been merged to main for at least 24 hours and a completed reconcile-bridge.yml run … Record the A2-1 merge SHA, workflow run id, and git merge-base --is-ancestor result on A2-2 before merge.'
scenarios: A contributor opens A2-2 and merges it the same day as A2-1 (forgetting the gate). A reconcile-bridge.yml run picks up A2-2's code, stops writing the legacy inline field, and an older in-flight MCP or review-bot binary that reads only the inline field sees last_get_pass=0 and resets rotation state.
A6-1 is executed before A6-0a's descendant-workflow evidence is recorded. Stale-epoch clones (review-bot EBS, local tracker) merge silently instead of aborting, producing divergent ticket state.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a lightweight required CI job (e.g. `check-rollout-gate.yml`) that fails if the PR body does not contain the required SHA + run-ID + merge-base output tokens, or that queries the GitHub API to verify the A2-1 merge commit's descendant relationship and the existence of a completed workflow run descended from it. Mark the job as a required status check on the `main` branch for the A2-2 and A6-0a→A6-1 milestone PRs.

findings.location: Scope step A4-2 — 'A4-2 requires both the forward full->key-set corpus diff and the reverse key-set->full rollback diff before merge'; Compatibility and rollback section — 'A2-2 and A4-2 are irreversible expand/contract steps'.
scenarios: A4-2 is deployed and a bug in the narrowed prev_snapshot causes spurious Jira mutations. findings.finding: A6-0b ('make the persistent review-bot clone self-converge and fix its deploy trigger') is scope drift beyond what the title promises — 'make the committed .bridge_state cache cheap + one-time reclaim'. It is a bug-fix/infra change to the review-bot deploy pipeline that is neither a cache-cheapness change nor part of the history reclaim. The plan justifies it as necessary because an src/rebar/ change activates the deploy path, but this justification makes it a deployment prerequisite, not a content/cost-reduction measure. If this prerequisite is truly load-bearing it should be a named dependency, not folded silently into the cache-reduction epic.

scenarios: A reader scanning the plan to scope A6 work will discover an unrelated review-bot deploy-trigger fix bundled inside A6-0b without a clear causal chain from 'cache cheap' to 'deploy trigger fix', risking unexpected scope during implementation.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Evaluate splitting A6-0b into two children: one for the review-bot self-convergence logic and one for the deploy trigger fix, since each is independently valuable, testable, and releasable — unless the deploy trigger fix is genuinely trivial (a single-line change) and inseparable from the convergence PR in practice.
evidence: Plan text: 'A6-0b make the persistent review-bot clone self-converge and fix its deploy trigger; it ships with A6-0a so an src/rebar/ change activates the deploy path'
The plan's own coupling rationale ('so an src/rebar/ change activates the deploy path') is a deploy-trigger concern, not a self-convergence concern — confirming they are distinct.
Self-convergence is independently valuable: the bot recovers from drift regardless of whether the reclaim has happened.
Deploy-trigger fix is independently valuable: any future rebar change benefits from it whether or not self-convergence is implemented.
findings.finding: A6-0b bundles two independently releasable and independently testable concerns: (1) making the review-bot's tickets clone self-converge (a behavioral resilience feature, valuable on its own) and (2) fixing the deploy trigger (an operational CI fix, independently valuable for any future src/rebar/ change). These have distinct reasons to change and distinct personas (application developer vs. ops/deploy owner), satisfying the single-concern decomposition trigger.
findings.location: Scope section, item 10: 'A6-0b make the persistent review-bot clone self-converge and fix its deploy trigger'
scenarios: If the deploy trigger fix is straightforward and ready but self-convergence needs design iteration, bundling them blocks the easier fix from landing.
If a regression is introduced in self-convergence logic, the deploy trigger fix is also held back or rolled back together, increasing blast radius.
Different team members may own deploy infra vs. bot application logic, creating coordination overhead inside one ticket.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In A2-1, make the `max(new, legacy)` comparator explicit: state that pass_ids are lexicographically ordered ISO-8601 timestamps and that string `max()` is the correct recency comparator, or add an assertion/normalization that enforces this during the transition.
evidence: Plan text: 'read max(new, legacy)'

outbound_differ.py:597: `_absent_candidates.sort(key=lambda k: _last_get_pass(binding_store, k))` — sorts pass_ids ascending; the rotation correctness property depends on the sort order matching the recency order of pass_ids.
The plan does not state that pass_ids are ISO-8601 strings or that lexicographic max equals chronologically most-recent.
findings.finding: A2-1 specifies 'read `max(new, legacy)`' for `last_get_pass` during the transition window, but does not define the comparator. `last_get_pass` values are pass_id strings; the correct max is lexicographic, which equals chronological order only if pass_ids are strictly ISO-8601-formatted timestamps. The sort in `_absent_candidates.sort(key=lambda k: _last_get_pass(binding_store, k))` at `outbound_differ.py:597` is ascending-alphabetic; if pass_ids are not strictly ISO-timestamp-ordered, `max(new, legacy)` could elect the wrong rotation bookmark and stall a key in an incorrect GET-rotation position during the A2-1→A2-2 transition window.

scenarios: If pass_id format ever changes to a non-ISO string (e.g., a UUID or monotonic integer), `max()` of the string forms produces an incorrect result during the transition window, electing an older pass_id as 'more recent' and incorrectly delaying a GET for a key.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one sentence to A2-1's spec: 'Pass_ids are ISO-8601 UTC strings; lexicographic `max()` equals chronological recency. Assert or normalize the format at read time if the source is the legacy inline field.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Ground the quiescence sequencing protocol (A6-0d → A6-1) in prior art for coordinated force-push windows on multi-writer git branches (e.g., BFG Repo Cleaner runbooks, GitLab/Linux kernel coordinated rewrite procedures, or the crates.io force-with-lease squash script), or explicitly document why no applicable prior art exists and what makes the custom protocol sufficient.
evidence: Plan: 'Its mechanics are proven: a length-aware git fast-export --no-data | filter | git fast-import pipeline on the real branch'

Session log [3/3]: 'KEY DISQUALIFIER FOUND: every squash case had exactly ONE writer. rebar's tickets branch is multi-writer... No prior art exists for a squash on a merge-replicated multi-writer branch.'

Session log [3/3]: 'RECLAIM: initially dropped on that basis, then RE-ADMITTED by operator decision under an explicit quiescence protocol (paused schedulers + confirmed zero sessions = single-writer for the duration, which IS the precondition prior art required).'

Session log [3/3] E1: 'Quiescence alone does NOT close it' (the unrelated-histories hazard) — then re-designs around a different mechanism; the quiescence sequencing itself has no cited prior-art basis.

ABSENCE: The plan cites no prior-art source for the specific quiescence sequencing (disable workflows → pause review-bot/autodeploy → poll for zero in-flight → operator attestation → force-with-lease), which is the novel element enabling the reuse of single-writer prior art.
findings.finding: The plan's quiescence protocol for the multi-writer history rewrite (A6-1) is presented as the key enabler that makes prior single-writer squash art applicable, but the protocol's own design is not grounded in any prior art for coordinated force-push windows on multi-writer git branches. The session log itself records that the original hazard mechanism (E1: unrelated histories) was mis-identified, yet the quiescence sequencing that replaced it is not cross-referenced to any established pattern (e.g., BFG Repo Cleaner operational guides, GitLab/Linux kernel coordinated force-push procedures). The claim that pausing schedulers + zero-session attestation + force-with-lease fully closes the multi-writer hazard relies on a novel protocol design without prior-art grounding.
findings.location: Approach section ('operator-approved quiescence protocol'), A6-1 scope item, Compatibility/rollback section (5-step rollback), session_log 1cb6-d553-6565-49b4 comment [3/3]
scenarios: A step in the quiescence protocol fails silently (e.g., an in-flight workflow run is not detected by polling), leaving a concurrent writer active during the rewrite window — a scenario the protocol claims to close but that has no prior-art validation of the polling approach.

The operator attestation covers MCP sessions but not other write paths (e.g., a scheduled workflow that was disabled but re-enabled by an infra change during the window), reproducing the E2 push.py bypass pattern in a quiescence context.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Verify whether git-filter-repo is available on the GitHub Actions runner environment used for A6-0c, and if so, re-evaluate the dependency rationale; if the custom pipeline is retained, document how commit-message corruption (the known grep-stream caveat) is guarded against (e.g., anchoring path-match patterns to line-start M/D prefixes only).
evidence: Plan: 'Stock git plumbing is used because it is already available and proven for this repository, avoiding a new third-party core dependency. git-filter-repo could preserve empty commits with --prune-empty=never; DAG preservation is therefore not a reason to reject it.'

git-filter-repo README (github.com/newren/git-filter-repo): the grep/regex approach 'might accidentally corrupt unintended portions of it, such as commit messages' and 'will leave behind huge numbers of useless empty commits, and has no realistic way of pruning them' — documented caveats for the exact pipeline pattern the plan describes.
git-filter-repo is distributed as a single Python script, included in major Linux distros, and listed by git-scm.com documentation as the recommended alternative to filter-branch.
ABSENCE: The plan does not check whether git-filter-repo is pre-installed on GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runners, which would make the 'new dependency' argument moot for A6-0c.
findings.finding: The plan rejects git-filter-repo in favour of a custom grep/stream pipeline primarily on the grounds of 'avoiding a new third-party core dependency', but does not verify whether git-filter-repo is already available on GitHub-hosted runners (where A6-0c tooling would be built/dry-run), nor does it consider the well-documented risk that the grep-based fast-export stream filter 'might accidentally corrupt unintended portions of it, such as commit messages' (a caveat explicitly called out in the git-filter-repo README for the pattern the plan describes). The plan acknowledges filter-repo's --prune-empty=never capability but does not engage with filter-repo's correctness properties vs. the custom pipeline's known stream-corruption risk.
findings.location: Approach section ('Stock git plumbing is used because it is already available and proven for this repository, avoiding a new third-party core dependency')
scenarios: The grep-based stream filter inadvertently matches a path pattern inside a commit message (e.g., a commit message mentioning '.bridge_state' as a path), corrupting the rewritten history in a way that is not caught until after publication.
git-filter-repo is already present on the GitHub Actions runner environment, making the 'new dependency' rejection moot and leaving the plan with an unjustified choice of a riskier custom pipeline.
findings.suggested_fix: Anchor all grep/sed patterns in the fast-export stream filter to the start of file-path lines (e.g., `^[MD] [0-9]+ [0-9a-f]+ \.bridge_state`) rather than unanchored substrings, and add a post-filter sanity check that commit-count and merge-count in the output stream match the input before piping to fast-import.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the A4-2 post-rollback prev_snapshot reconstruction procedure: either (a) name git history as the recovery source (e.g., `git show <pre-A4-2-tip>:.bridge_state/prev_snapshot.json > prev_snapshot.json`) and add this to the child ticket's rollback steps, or (b) specify a Jira re-fetch as the recovery path, and confirm both are exercised in the pre-merge dry-run.
evidence: Plan: 'A4-2 narrow prev_snapshot.json to a key-set after A4-1; record forward and reverse corpus mutation diffs before merge'
Plan: 'A2-2 and A4-2 are irreversible expand/contract steps'
Session log [1/3]: 'key-set payload at HEAD = 19,960 bytes vs 27.1 MB full' — the key-set carries no field values
reconcile.py:271: prev_snapshot consumed as a dict of {jira_key: field_dict}; a key-set file with no field values yields empty dicts per key, causing the differ to treat all fields as absent
Plan's Compatibility and rollback section specifies a 5-step procedure for A6-1 history strip only; no procedure for A4-2 post-rollback prev_snapshot reconstruction is given
ABSENCE: the plan does not state 'recover the prior prev_snapshot from git history' or 're-fetch from Jira' as the A4-2 rollback recovery mechanism
findings.finding: A4-2 narrows prev_snapshot.json from full Jira field data (~27 MB, containing field values for all 1509 bindings) to a key-set only (~20 KB, containing only Jira keys). After a reconciler pass writes the key-set format, the full Jira field payloads are permanently absent from the working tree. The plan's rollback artifact is a 'reverse key-set->full corpus diff,' but this diff captures only key-set membership changes (which keys were added or removed), NOT the actual field values (summary, description, priority, status, assignee). Rolling back the A4-2 code change (reverting to the pre-A4-2 reader) while the store carries a key-set prev_snapshot.json leaves the reader with no usable field data: the differ treats all field values as absent and re-derives spurious inbound-create or field-update mutations for all bound tickets. The plan does not specify how to reconstruct the full prev_snapshot.json after A4-2 is live (e.g., recover from git history — which IS available at this point since A6-1 runs later — or re-fetch from Jira).
findings.location: Scope item A4-2; Compatibility and rollback section; AC line 'Full-prev versus key-set-prev corpus mutation diff … the reverse-direction diff is recorded too'
scenarios: A4-2 merges and one reconciler pass runs; a production issue is discovered; A4-2 is reverted; the next pass reads the key-set prev_snapshot.json with the old code and re-derives 1509+ spurious inbound-create/field-update mutations, sending incorrect updates to Jira for all bound tickets.

An operator performs A4-2 rollback under pressure; the reverse-direction diff artifact is available but contains only Jira key additions/removals (not field values); applying it does not restore a usable prev_snapshot.json for the pre-A4-2 reader.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the A4-2 child ticket's rollback section: 'On A4-2 revert, restore the full prev_snapshot.json from git history: `git show <A4-2-pre-merge-tip>:.bridge_state/prev_snapshot.json > .tickets-tracker/.bridge_state/prev_snapshot.json && git add -f .tickets-tracker/.bridge_state/prev_snapshot.json && git commit -m "rollback: restore full prev_snapshot for A4-2 revert"`. Verify the restored file is valid JSON with field values (not just keys) before re-enabling the reconciler. Record the pre-A4-2 tip SHA in the A4-2 child ticket before merge.'
